analysis.one_liner: Bans contract clauses that stop health insurers and employers from seeing and sharing prices and quality data.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with bipartisan sponsorship in February 2020, was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and died there without a hearing, a markup, or any floor vote before Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would bar health insurers, employer health plans, and providers from signing contracts that hide price and quality information. It stops so-called "gag clauses" — terms that keep insurers from telling employers or patients what providers actually charge, or from seeing the full claims data behind their own plans. It also requires plans to certify each year that their contracts don't contain these secrecy terms. The goal is to let employers and patients comparison-shop and spot overcharges. The bill never got a vote: after its introduction it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and remained there until the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers who sponsor health plans — especially self-insured employers that pay their workers' medical bills directly — would gain the right to see provider-specific prices, full claims data, and quality information that contracts now often block. Enrollees would get access to provider-specific cost and quality information, making it possible to compare prices before treatment. Referring doctors would see what other providers charge, helping them steer patients to lower-priced care.

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits group health plans and insurers from entering any provider or network agreement that restricts them from providing provider-specific cost or quality information to referring providers, plan sponsors, and enrollees [S2] [S3].

Plans and insurers could no longer be blocked from electronically accessing de-identified claims and encounter data — including the allowed amounts, provider names, and service codes on each claim — upon request, consistent with federal privacy rules [S3].
The bill requires plans and insurers to submit an annual attestation to federal regulators that they are complying with these transparency requirements [S3].

The bill permits plans to share this information with business associates for plan administration and quality improvement, while leaving providers free to place reasonable restrictions on fully public disclosure of the data [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Hospital systems, provider networks, and third-party administrators that currently use contract terms to keep negotiated prices and claims data hidden would lose that secrecy. Insurers and plan administrators would face new compliance work, including annual attestation filings. The costs would likely surface as harder negotiations: providers could no longer rely on opacity to protect above-market rates.
analysis.who_pays_short: Hospitals and plan administrators relying on secrecy

drawbacks.text: Price transparency alone may not lower costs if patients cannot act on the information in emergencies, or if a few large hospital systems dominate a local market and patients have no alternatives to comparison-shop among [S3].

The bill relies on annual self-attestation rather than audits or penalties, so enforcement depends on plans honestly certifying compliance, and the introduced version includes no funding or enforcement mechanism beyond the attestation itself [S3].

Hospitals and provider networks argue that forced disclosure of negotiated contract rates could weaken their negotiating position, raising administrative friction and potentially leading providers to demand higher initial rates to offset reduced bargaining secrecy — a cost that could ultimately be passed to premiums, though this is contested [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addresses a real and documented problem — contract terms that block employers and patients from seeing what care actually costs — and it does so narrowly, respecting privacy rules and allowing reasonable limits on public disclosure. Its main weaknesses are enforcement (self-attestation, no audits or penalties) and the possibility that transparency alone won't discipline provider prices in markets dominated by one or two hospital systems. On balance, it is a modest, well-targeted transparency measure whose costs fall mainly on entities that benefit from price opacity.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late February 2020, referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Representative Tom Malinowski introduced the bill on February 27, 2020, with Representative Larry Bucshon as the sole cosponsor [S1] [S3] [S4].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on the day it was introduced, and the action history shows no further activity after that referral [S5] [S1].
The bill never advanced to the floor and expired when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals, provider networks, and plan administrators who benefit from contract terms keeping negotiated prices and claims data hidden from employers and patients are better off, because the bill never received a vote or became law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Providers and administrators keeping prices hidden

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship (one Democrat, one Republican), but it drew no recorded opposition because it never advanced to a hearing, markup, or vote.

industries.note: Hospital systems and provider groups commonly used contract terms restricting what plans could share about their negotiated prices and quality; the bill bans those gag clauses. Losing that opacity would expose their negotiated rates to employers, patients, and referring physicians, weakening their ability to protect above-market rates.

industries.industry: Third-party administrators and network access firms
industries.note: These firms provide access to provider networks and often structure the data-restriction agreements the bill prohibits. They would lose business arrangements built around keeping claims and price data from plan sponsors.

Insurers would face new attestation and data-sharing obligations, but the bill also guarantees their access to de-identified claims and encounter data they are currently sometimes barred from seeing. Their interest in transparency runs alongside employers' and patients' here, since the secrecy terms being banned bind insurers too.

Self-insured employers paying their workers' medical bills directly would gain the right to full claims data and provider-specific prices, letting them audit what they are paying for and negotiate more effectively.
